<a id="rule-d2f86e75-7692-468e-88a2-52eb1e24dc30"></a>

#### The speculative-execution mitigations are switched off

- Id: `d2f86e75-7692-468e-88a2-52eb1e24dc30`
- File: [`rules/posture/mitigations/speculative-execution-mitigations-disabled/rule.yaml`](../rules/posture/mitigations/speculative-execution-mitigations-disabled/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `posture`
- Strength: `posture`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `posture`, `mitigations`
- Written: 2026-09-21

**About this check**

Windows is told to turn off the mitigations for Spectre variant 2 and Meltdown, by the pair of values that together mean off. The mitigations cost a few percent of performance, and turning them off is a step several gaming tweak scripts take; it also leaves the PC exposed to the processor flaws they were written for. It is a setting the owner of the machine chose and it is not evidence of cheating.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `speculative_execution_mitigations`: is `disabled` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Current state only. It says nothing about how the PC was set up in the past.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows
- `access_denied` — Windows refused to open this

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- An owner who followed performance advice for an older processor, on which these mitigations cost the most
- A tweaking script or a pre-modified Windows image the owner installed for performance
- A PC set up this way by a shop or by whoever built it

**References**

- <https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/topic/kb4073119-windows-client-guidance-for-it-pros-to-protect-against-silicon-based-microarchitectural-and-speculative-execution-side-channel-vulnerabilities-35820a8a-ae13-1299-88cc-357f104f5b11>

### `posture` / `tpm`

<a id="rule-66d513b5-fe61-415a-9385-9d01f85c3ef5"></a>

#### No TPM is present

- Id: `66d513b5-fe61-415a-9385-9d01f85c3ef5`
- File: [`rules/posture/tpm/tpm-absent/rule.yaml`](../rules/posture/tpm/tpm-absent/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `posture`
- Strength: `context`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `posture`, `tpm`
- Written: 2026-09-12

**About this check**

The platform reports that this machine has no TPM. A TPM is one of the stable pieces of hardware an identity can be tied to, so whether one exists is useful background when a reviewer is reading the rest of a report. Enormous numbers of working PCs have no TPM at all or have it switched off in firmware, so this says nothing about the person using the machine and is not evidence of cheating.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `tpm`: is `absent` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Current hardware state only. It says nothing about earlier hardware or firmware settings.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- PCs built without a TPM, which includes a great many older and self-assembled machines
- A TPM switched off or hidden in firmware, which is a common factory default
- Virtual machines and test systems that have no virtual TPM attached

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/hardware-security/tpm/trusted-platform-module-overview>

## Collector `powershell_text`

### `powershell_text` / `engine-start`

<a id="rule-1fd8ec4a-f6d1-4496-aac5-54ed276717f7"></a>

#### A command in a Windows PowerShell start told Microsoft Defender to look away

- Id: `1fd8ec4a-f6d1-4496-aac5-54ed276717f7`
- File: [`rules/powershell_text/engine-start/defender-tamper/rule.yaml`](../rules/powershell_text/engine-start/defender-tamper/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `powershell_text`
- Strength: `tamper`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `powershell_text`
- Written: 2026-10-08

**About this check**

In the command lines Windows PowerShell was started with, as its own log keeps them, at least one command added an exclusion to Microsoft Defender or switched one of its protections off. The report also says what Defender is told not to scan now, when the scan has administrator rights. This tool reads the command only to sort its words into kinds and keeps no text of it, so the row says what kind of words it held, never which command, what it ran or whether it worked. A word built some other way than PowerShell's ordinary escapes is not recognised, so a missing row says nothing.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `defender_tamper`: is `true`
- `source`: is `engine_start` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Only the starts the Windows PowerShell log still holds. It keeps 15 MiB by default and overwrites its oldest records when full; on one Windows 11 PC that was about six days. A cleared log holds none.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows
- `source_absent` — this PC has no such record to read

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- Developers and IT staff excluding build folders or tools to speed Defender up
- Game, emulator or mod guides that tell players to exclude a folder
- Turning protection off to install a program Defender flagged by mistake
- A missing row does not mean Defender was never changed, since its own settings and log say more

**References**

- <https://github.com/aeterna/aeterna-rongroi/blob/dev/docs/adr/0064-words-in-powershell-commands-never-the-commands.md>

<a id="rule-45a6c6d4-6759-48c0-82e6-4cafb2ea2bfb"></a>

#### A command in a Windows PowerShell start downloaded something and ran it

- Id: `45a6c6d4-6759-48c0-82e6-4cafb2ea2bfb`
- File: [`rules/powershell_text/engine-start/download-then-execute/rule.yaml`](../rules/powershell_text/engine-start/download-then-execute/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `powershell_text`
- Strength: `presence`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `powershell_text`
- Written: 2026-10-08

**About this check**

In the command lines Windows PowerShell was started with, as its own log keeps them, at least one command held both a word that downloads from the internet and a word that runs text as a command, the shape of a line that fetches a script and runs it without saving it. The row gives how many and the first and last time, and the website's name only if the player agreed to show it. This tool reads the command only to sort its words into kinds and keeps no text of it, so the row says what kind of words it held, never which command, what it ran or whether it worked. A word built some other way than PowerShell's ordinary escapes is not recognised, so a missing row says nothing.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `download_then_execute`: is `true`
- `source`: is `engine_start` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Only the starts the Windows PowerShell log still holds. It keeps 15 MiB by default and overwrites its oldest records when full; on one Windows 11 PC that was about six days. A cleared log holds none.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows
- `source_absent` — this PC has no such record to read

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- Installers and package managers that are installed with one line of this shape — the measured development PC's history held three, all from installing software
- Scripts that update or set up developer tools, terminals or Windows tweaks the same way
- A program or a scheduled task that starts PowerShell this way to update itself
- A missing row does not mean nothing was run, because other ways of running a script are not read

**References**

- <https://github.com/aeterna/aeterna-rongroi/blob/dev/docs/adr/0064-words-in-powershell-commands-never-the-commands.md>

<a id="rule-a5b02d12-4999-4cd6-87cc-c7823aee66b9"></a>

#### A command in a Windows PowerShell start cleared a log, the history or Prefetch

- Id: `a5b02d12-4999-4cd6-87cc-c7823aee66b9`
- File: [`rules/powershell_text/engine-start/trace-cleanup/rule.yaml`](../rules/powershell_text/engine-start/trace-cleanup/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `powershell_text`
- Strength: `tamper`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `powershell_text`

**About this check**

In the command lines Windows PowerShell was started with, as its own log keeps them, at least one command cleared PowerShell's history, cleared or removed an event log, or deleted the history file or files under Prefetch. This tool reads the command only to sort its words into kinds and keeps no text of it, so the row says what kind of words it held, never which command, what it ran or whether it worked. A word built some other way than PowerShell's ordinary escapes is not recognised, so a missing row says nothing.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `source`: is `engine_start` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `trace_cleanup`: is `true`

**Look-back**

Only the starts the Windows PowerShell log still holds. It keeps 15 MiB by default and overwrites its oldest records when full; on one Windows 11 PC that was about six days. A cleared log holds none.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows
- `source_absent` — this PC has no such record to read

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- A person clearing their own command history

- A missing row does not mean nothing was cleared, because other tools leave no line here

**References**

- <https://github.com/aeterna/aeterna-rongroi/blob/dev/docs/adr/0064-words-in-powershell-commands-never-the-commands.md>

### `powershell_text` / `history`

<a id="rule-b97cb4c6-9dac-47f4-a974-ce17f07d6fc5"></a>

- Collector: `powershell_text`
- Strength: `tamper`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `powershell_text`
- Written: 2026-10-08

**About this check**

In the history of commands typed into a PowerShell window on the account running this scan, at least one command added an exclusion to Microsoft Defender or switched one of its protections off. The report also says what Defender is told not to scan now, when the scan has administrator rights. This tool reads the command only to sort its words into kinds and keeps no text of it, so the row says what kind of words it held, never which command, what it ran or whether it worked. A word built some other way than PowerShell's ordinary escapes is not recognised, so a missing row says nothing.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `defender_tamper`: is `true`
- `source`: is `history` (text, ASCII case ignored)

Only the lines PowerShell's history file still holds. It keeps the newest 4096 commands by default and writes no time for a line, so the row says how many commands ago, not when. PowerShell leaves out of the file every line holding the words password, token, key or secret.

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows

- A missing row does not mean Defender was never changed, since its own settings and log say more
- A scan restarted with another administrator's password, which reads that administrator's history, not the person's at the keyboard; each row then says \`account: other\`

**References**

- <https://github.com/aeterna/aeterna-rongroi/blob/dev/docs/adr/0064-words-in-powershell-commands-never-the-commands.md>

## Collector `prefetch`

### `prefetch` / `file-attributes`

<a id="rule-7d493537-7ecf-4f97-90a0-119e079d30d2"></a>

#### A Prefetch file is marked read-only

- Id: `7d493537-7ecf-4f97-90a0-119e079d30d2`
- File: [`rules/prefetch/file-attributes/prefetch-file-read-only/rule.yaml`](../rules/prefetch/file-attributes/prefetch-file-read-only/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `prefetch`
- Strength: `tamper`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `prefetch`, `file-attributes`
- Written: 2026-09-13

**About this check**

A file in the Windows Prefetch folder carries the read-only attribute. Windows writes and rewrites these files itself, and on the one Windows 11 machine this project measured, none of them carried the attribute. This row names the file and what it records. It does not say who set the attribute, when, or why, and it is not evidence that anything was hidden or that the program it names was used to cheat.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `read_only`: is `true`

**Look-back**

The attribute as it is at the moment of the scan, on the Prefetch files still in the folder. It says nothing about when it was set, or about files that were removed.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows
- `not_admin` — Windows would not show this without administrator rights
- `source_absent` — this PC has no such record to read
- `service_disabled` — the Windows service that writes this record is switched off

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- Read-only chosen in the Properties of the Prefetch folder or of a folder above it, which Windows applies to the files inside
- Files copied or restored into the folder by backup, imaging or copy software that keeps file attributes, as Windows' own robocopy does unless told otherwise

**Related rules**

- similar to [An event log file is marked read-only](#rule-9b318bfa-805d-4edd-81f1-602b57639a69)

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/file-attribute-constants>

## Collector `process_modules`

### `process_modules` / `memory`

<a id="rule-d125476c-6df4-4a34-a61a-2b9741cf1cc1"></a>

#### A running process holds an executable image the Windows loader did not load

- Id: `d125476c-6df4-4a34-a61a-2b9741cf1cc1`
- File: [`rules/process_modules/memory/image-in-private-memory/rule.yaml`](../rules/process_modules/memory/image-in-private-memory/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `process_modules`
- Strength: `context`
- Status: `test` — believed correct; has a positive and a negative fixture
- Tags: `process`, `memory`, `injection`
- Written: 2026-10-16

**About this check**

Private executable memory in a running process begins with a PE image header: code copied into memory by hand rather than loaded by Windows. Manual-mapping injectors do this; so do some packers, runtimes and security products. The process and the address are on the row.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `holds_image`: is `true`
- `scope`: is `allocation` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

The address space at the moment of the scan.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows
- `access_denied` — Windows refused to open this

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- Packed or protected legitimate programs that unpack themselves into private memory
- Security products and anti-cheats that copy modules for inspection

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/memoryapi/nf-memoryapi-virtualqueryex>

### `process_modules` / `module`

<a id="rule-e3f4cb04-3fce-4104-b0ab-8a4bdf6797a1"></a>

#### A module loaded in a running process is suspicious or its integrity is compromised

- Id: `e3f4cb04-3fce-4104-b0ab-8a4bdf6797a1`
- File: [`rules/process_modules/module/loaded-module-integrity-not-trusted/rule.yaml`](../rules/process_modules/module/loaded-module-integrity-not-trusted/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `process_modules`
- Strength: `presence`
- Status: `test` — believed correct; has a positive and a negative fixture
- Tags: `process`, `module`, `integrity`
- Written: 2026-10-16

**About this check**

A DLL loaded in a running process was classified suspicious, integrity compromised or malicious with corroborated evidence. The reasons and the processes that loaded it are on the row. Most loaded modules are signed system or vendor files and are not listed.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `integrity_class`: is one of `suspicious`, `integrity_compromised`, `malicious_corroborated` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `scope`: is `module` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

The modules loaded at the moment of the scan.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows
- `access_denied` — Windows refused to open this

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- A debugger, profiler, macro tool or modding tool that imports process-writing functions
- A legitimate file whose signature became invalid after an interrupted update

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/psapi/nf-psapi-enumprocessmodulesex>

## Collector `roblox`

### `roblox` / `client-settings`

A ClientAppSettings.json file in a Roblox version folder sets one or more engine settings ("FastFlags"). Bootstrappers such as Bloxstrap write it to change graphics, frame-rate and lighting options, and Roblox honours only an allow-list of flags. Only the count is read, never the flags or values.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

### `roblox` / `player`

<a id="rule-d5e16389-ebfc-4885-adf7-f24e6bcd7b0c"></a>

#### RobloxPlayerBeta.exe has no embedded signature that verifies here

- Id: `d5e16389-ebfc-4885-adf7-f24e6bcd7b0c`
- File: [`rules/roblox/player/player-exe-without-verified-signature/rule.yaml`](../rules/roblox/player/player-exe-without-verified-signature/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `roblox`
- Strength: `presence`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `roblox`, `signature`
- Written: 2026-10-15

**About this check**

The Roblox player in a version folder under Versions carries no embedded Authenticode signature, one that does not verify, or one Windows could not verify without the internet; the row says which. The official player is signed by Roblox Corporation. This does not say the file was changed, what it does, or that it ran. "Could not verify without the internet" also covers a PC whose certificate store lacks the root the signature chains to.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `location`: is `player_exe` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `signature`: is one of `no_embedded_signature`, `invalid`, `unverifiable_offline` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

The file as it is at scan time. An update of Roblox replaces the version folder.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- A PC whose certificate store does not hold the root certificate, which Windows normally fetches online the first time it is needed; this check never goes online
- A player file damaged by an interrupted update, a disk problem or security software that partly quarantined it

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/seccrypto/authenticode>

<a id="rule-9888b00d-53c9-47ff-b719-2ed7c44b8fe1"></a>

#### A file named like a Windows system DLL sits beside the Roblox player

- Id: `9888b00d-53c9-47ff-b719-2ed7c44b8fe1`
- File: [`rules/roblox/player/system-dll-name-beside-player/rule.yaml`](../rules/roblox/player/system-dll-name-beside-player/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `roblox`
- Strength: `presence`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `roblox`, `dll-hijack`
- Written: 2026-10-15

**About this check**

A DLL with the name of a Windows system library (version.dll, dxgi.dll, winmm.dll and similar) sits directly in a Roblox version folder. Windows looks in the program's own folder before System32, so a file there with one of these names is loaded into the player instead of, or before, the real library: the "proxy DLL" technique. The official player does not ship these files. This does not say what the DLL does or that the player loaded it.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `location`: is `version_binary` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `name`: is one of `version.dll`, `dxgi.dll`, `d3d11.dll`, `d3d9.dll`, `winmm.dll`, `dinput8.dll`, `xinput1_3.dll`, `xinput1_4.dll`, `winhttp.dll`, `dwmapi.dll`, `opengl32.dll`, `wininet.dll`, `dbghelp.dll`, `dsound.dll` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

The version folder as it is at scan time.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- Graphics post-processing tools such as ReShade, which install themselves as dxgi.dll or d3d11.dll beside a game
- A file copied there by hand while troubleshooting a crash

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/dlls/dynamic-link-library-search-order>

<a id="rule-1a665dfa-9a53-4dcb-a9ec-942ac07d57e6"></a>

#### An unsigned program or DLL sits beside the Roblox player

- Id: `1a665dfa-9a53-4dcb-a9ec-942ac07d57e6`
- File: [`rules/roblox/player/unsigned-binary-beside-player/rule.yaml`](../rules/roblox/player/unsigned-binary-beside-player/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `roblox`
- Strength: `presence`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `roblox`, `signature`
- Written: 2026-10-15

**About this check**

A .dll, .exe or .asi file directly in a Roblox version folder carries no embedded signature, or one that does not verify. Roblox signs the binaries it ships; a file without a signature there was most likely put there by something else. It does not say what the file does or that it was loaded.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `location`: is `version_binary` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `signature`: is one of `no_embedded_signature`, `invalid` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

The version folder as it is at scan time.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- A Roblox binary signed through a Windows catalog rather than embedded, which this check does not read; not observed for Roblox
- Graphics or overlay tools that drop a DLL into game folders

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/seccrypto/authenticode>

## Collector `roblox_flags`

### `roblox_flags` / `change`

<a id="rule-be178c93-0089-47af-8571-a384b17ee4bc"></a>

#### Another copy of the Roblox settings held a non-reference value the active file no longer has

- Id: `be178c93-0089-47af-8571-a384b17ee4bc`

**About this check**

A backup, an older version folder or a bootstrapper's copy sets a flag to a value that differs from the reference, while the active version's file now holds the reference value or does not set the flag. That is what setting a flag and putting it back leaves on disk. Both files and both modification times are on the row; no other time is inferred, and it does not say when the value was in effect.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `scope`: is `change` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- An old version folder Roblox has not removed yet, from before the player reset their settings
- A bootstrapper profile the player no longer uses

**References**

- <https://github.com/MaximumADHD/Roblox-FFlag-Tracker>

### `roblox_flags` / `dump`

A crash dump the Roblox player left holds a FastFlag assignment written as JSON text that sets a network or physics flag to a value different from the reference. A ClientAppSettings.json in a Roblox version folder, or a bootstrapper's copy of it, sets a network or physics flag (PhysicsSenderRate, replication or humanoid flags) to a value that differs from the FFlag tracker reference. ## Collector `roblox_memory`

### `roblox_memory` / `code`

<a id="rule-917fecbb-4032-4fae-9091-4ccd4417b0bd"></a>

#### Code of a module in the Roblox player differs from its file

- Id: `917fecbb-4032-4fae-9091-4ccd4417b0bd`
- File: [`rules/roblox_memory/code/module-code-differs-from-file/rule.yaml`](../rules/roblox_memory/code/module-code-differs-from-file/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `roblox_memory`
- Strength: `context`
- Status: `test` — believed correct; has a positive and a negative fixture
- Tags: `roblox`, `memory`, `integrity`
- Written: 2026-10-16

**About this check**

The executable sections of a module loaded in the running Roblox player were compared with its file, laid out and relocated as Windows loads it, with the tables the loader fills skipped, and some bytes differ. Patched code looks like this; so do hooks placed by overlays, capture tools and security software. Roblox's own image is excluded because its anti-cheat changes it at run time. The row gives how many bytes differ and where.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `bytes_differing|gte`: is at least `1`
- `expected_runtime_change`: is `false`
- `scope`: is `code_change` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

The code in memory at the moment of the scan.

### `roblox_memory` / `hook`

<a id="rule-cd24dd82-84f7-4793-87ad-3b34234387ba"></a>

**About this check**

The first bytes of a function exported by a module loaded in the running Roblox player differ from the module's file and now jump to private or mapped memory that no loaded module accounts for. Inline hooks placed by injected code look like this. Overlays, recorders and security software also hook functions, but they usually jump into their own signed module. Roblox's own image is excluded here because its anti-cheat changes it at run time. It shows the jump and where it goes; it does not say what the code there does.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `expected_runtime_change`: is `false`
- `scope`: is `hook` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `target_module|startswith`: starts with `unbacked_` (text, ASCII case ignored)

The code in memory at the moment of the scan.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows
- `access_denied` — Windows refused to open this
- `source_absent` — this PC has no such record to read

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- An overlay or capture tool that allocates its trampolines in private memory instead of inside its own module
- Security software or an anti-cheat that hooks system DLLs from memory it allocated

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/memoryapi/nf-memoryapi-readprocessmemory>

<a id="rule-719dca43-ca1f-4a18-b9c2-d5bd2a13b6a0"></a>

#### An unsigned program is running from Temp, Downloads, Desktop or the Recycle Bin

- Id: `719dca43-ca1f-4a18-b9c2-d5bd2a13b6a0`
- File: [`rules/roblox_process/user-location/unsigned-process-in-user-folder/rule.yaml`](../rules/roblox_process/user-location/unsigned-process-in-user-folder/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `roblox_process`
- Strength: `presence`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `process`, `signature`
- Written: 2026-10-15

**About this check**

A process running at scan time was started from Temp, Downloads, Desktop, the Public profile or the Recycle Bin, and its file carries no embedded signature or one that does not verify. Loaders and injectors are usually run this way; so are portable tools and freshly downloaded installers.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `location_kind`: is one of `temp`, `user_downloads`, `user_desktop`, `recycle_bin`, `users_public` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `scope`: is `user_location_process` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `signature`: is one of `no_embedded_signature`, `invalid` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Processes running at the moment of the scan.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- Portable tools, game mods and small utilities run straight from Downloads or the Desktop
- An installer still running from Downloads

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/seccrypto/authenticode>

## Collector `roblox_trace`

- Written: 2026-10-15

**About this check**

BAM, Amcache, ShimCache, UserAssist or a shortcut records a path to a file named like a Roblox executor or injector, and nothing is at that path today. It may have been moved, renamed, deleted or kept on a drive that is not connected; this does not say which.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `exists`: is `false`
- `roblox_context`: is `true`
- `scope`: is `hit` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Each history source's own retention; the file system as it is at scan time.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

The rule names none.

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- Strength: `context`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `roblox`, `history`
- Written: 2026-10-15

**About this check**

The Recycle Bin holds a deleted item, or the NTFS change journal holds a deletion record, for a file whose name matches a Roblox executor or injector. Deleting a file is ordinary; the row is a reason to ask what it was.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `evidence_class`: is `deleted` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `scope`: is `hit` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `tool_kind`: is one of `executor`, `injector` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

The Recycle Bin until emptied; the change journal until its oldest records are overwritten.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

The rule names none.

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- Removing a download one decided not to use

### `roblox_trace` / `tool`

<a id="rule-73592699-8fc5-468d-a22d-17ccb6898b15"></a>

#### A Roblox executor or injector is corroborated by independent sources

- Id: `73592699-8fc5-468d-a22d-17ccb6898b15`
- File: [`rules/roblox_trace/tool/corroborated/rule.yaml`](../rules/roblox_trace/tool/corroborated/rule.yaml)

- Strength: `presence`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `roblox`, `correlation`
- Written: 2026-10-15

**About this check**

The correlation of every source this scan read found one Roblox script executor or DLL injector, by name in a Roblox context, in two or more independent source families, with at least one showing it ran (Prefetch, BAM, PCA, UserAssist, FeatureUsage, a running process), an executor folder layout, executor-only scripts, or a module in the Roblox player. The row lists the families, the evidence classes and the earliest and latest times. Names can be copied and files renamed; times close together do not show cause.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `scope`: is `tool` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `status`: is `corroborated` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Whatever the sources read in this scan still hold; the sources table says which could not be read.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

The rule names none.

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- A name shared with unrelated software, or a file named this way on purpose; a legitimate tool renamed to match
- Files kept from the past, before the account or PC was used for play

## Collector `shellbags`

### `shellbags` / `dialog`

**About this check**

The common Open/Save dialog's list (OpenSavePidlMRU) holds a path whose file or folder name matches a Roblox executor or injector: a program used the dialog to open or save it. It is not proof that the file ran, nor which program used the dialog.

- `list`: is `open_save` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `tool_kind`: is one of `executor`, `injector` (text, ASCII case ignored)

### `shellbags` / `shellbag`

<a id="rule-1a7a3594-5b68-4142-8426-96aa0e0a2e90"></a>

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `list`: is `shellbag` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `tool_kind`: is one of `executor`, `injector` (text, ASCII case ignored)

ShellBags last until the account's profile is deleted or the history is cleared; Windows keeps thousands of folders.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `access_denied` — Windows refused to open this

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

## Collector `shimcache`

### `shimcache` / `location`

<a id="rule-71839ff2-255a-4df3-8014-de800fd4ffa1"></a>

#### A program in Temp or the Recycle Bin: the compatibility engine recorded the file (not proof it ran)

- Id: `71839ff2-255a-4df3-8014-de800fd4ffa1`
- File: [`rules/shimcache/location/program-in-temp-or-recycle-bin/rule.yaml`](../rules/shimcache/location/program-in-temp-or-recycle-bin/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `shimcache`
- Strength: `context`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `execution`
- Written: 2026-10-15

**About this check**

For a file in a Temp folder or the Recycle Bin, the compatibility engine recorded the file (not proof it ran). Programs rarely run from the Recycle Bin, and loaders often unpack to Temp before running; installers and updaters also run from Temp. Context for the timeline, never a finding on its own.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `location_kind`: is one of `temp`, `recycle_bin` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Up to 1 024 entries, written at shutdown; files seen since the last restart are usually missing.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows
- `source_absent` — this PC has no such record to read

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

## Collector `srum`

### `srum` / `app`

<a id="rule-e3f5c638-81e3-410a-9f1d-fe762b9f8731"></a>

#### SRUM recorded CPU time for a program named like a Roblox executor or injector

- Id: `e3f5c638-81e3-410a-9f1d-fe762b9f8731`
- File: [`rules/srum/app/executor-named-program-used-cpu/rule.yaml`](../rules/srum/app/executor-named-program-used-cpu/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `srum`
- Strength: `execution`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `roblox`, `srum`
- Written: 2026-10-15

**About this check**

The System Resource Usage Monitor database (SRUDB.dat, read from an existing shadow copy) holds rows saying that a program whose file name matches a Roblox executor or injector used CPU time, with the first and last hour it was recorded. SRUM writes about once an hour, so the times are hours, not starts. A name is not proof of what the program was, and the database misses whatever SRUM had not written yet when the shadow copy was taken.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `scope`: is `app` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `tool_kind`: is one of `executor`, `injector` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `used_cpu`: is `true`

**Look-back**

SRUM keeps about 30 to 60 days of hourly rows; a shadow copy is as old as the snapshot, and nothing after it is in the copy.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_admin` — Windows would not show this without administrator rights
- `source_absent` — this PC has no such record to read

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- An unrelated program that happens to carry the same file name, such as a game or utility called Solara or Wave
- A file renamed to a tool's name by someone testing this scanner

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/w8cookbook/system-resource-usage-monitor>

## Collector `usb_device`

### `usb_device` / `dev-board`

<a id="rule-3daec665-7482-4667-a268-3be496783a83"></a>

#### A microcontroller board has been a keyboard or mouse on this PC

- Id: `3daec665-7482-4667-a268-3be496783a83`
- File: [`rules/usb_device/dev-board/dev-board-as-input-device/rule.yaml`](../rules/usb_device/dev-board/dev-board-as-input-device/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `usb_device`
- Strength: `presence`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `usb`, `hid`, `badusb`
- Written: 2026-10-15

**About this check**

Windows' device list has a keyboard, mouse or other input device whose vendor id belongs to a maker of microcontroller and development boards (Arduino, SparkFun, Adafruit, Raspberry Pi, Teensy's shared id and others), present now or remembered. Input-automation and "Bad USB" devices are built on such boards. The row shows whether it is connected and its install, arrival and removal times. Windows does not log what a keyboard typed, and a board can claim any vendor id.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `bus`: is `hid` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `dev_board_vendor`: is `true`

**Look-back**

Devices Windows still remembers; a device removed with a cleanup tool or before a reinstall is not seen.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- Hand-built mechanical keyboards, macro pads and flight-simulator button boxes, which are commonly built on Arduino Pro Micro or RP2040 boards
- Electronics hobby projects that act as a keyboard or game controller

Devices Windows still remembers.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows

- 3D printers, flashing cables, hobby electronics and microcontroller programming

A program or DLL in Downloads, Desktop or Documents carries Windows' Mark of the Web for the Internet zone and has no embedded signature that verifies. Shown with its hash and, when the player agreed, the host it came from. Many ordinary downloads are unsigned.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `kind`: is `program` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `signature`: is one of `no_embedded_signature`, `invalid` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `zone_id`: is `3`

**Look-back**

The files as they are at scan time.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- Mods, indie games, open-source tools and utilities, which are often unsigned

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/openspecs/windows_protocols/ms-fscc/6e3f7352-d11c-4d76-8c39-2516a9df36e8>

## Collector `usn`

### `usn` / `enhanced-asi`

<a id="rule-1c73241b-b7f1-4f91-81d4-8de53db6d119"></a>

#### The change journal holds a deletion in FiveM for GTA V Enhanced's asi folder

- Id: `1c73241b-b7f1-4f91-81d4-8de53db6d119`
- File: [`rules/usn/enhanced-asi/files-deleted/rule.yaml`](../rules/usn/enhanced-asi/files-deleted/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `usn`
- Strength: `context`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `usn`, `enhanced_asi`
- Written: 2026-09-30

**About this check**

The NTFS change journal holds at least one record of a file deleted directly inside FiveM for GTA V Enhanced's asi folder. The row gives how many records, and the first and last time. It shows the span the journal covered: on an ordinary PC in use that can be well under an hour. Nothing before that span is seen. If this rule finds nothing, it means only that nothing was deleted there within that span. The journal does not record which program changed a file, so this does not say who did it, or that anything was hidden. Whether FiveM for GTA V Enhanced loads anything from this folder is not established.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `deleted|gte`: is at least `1`
- `folder`: is `identified` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `location`: is `enhanced_asi` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Only the span the change journal still held when the scan read it, shown beside this row. The journal keeps a fixed size and drops its oldest records first; on one Windows 11 PC it held about 39 minutes.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows
- `source_absent` — this PC has no such record to read
- `other_volume` — this is on another drive, and this program reads only the system drive's change journal

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- The player removed or replaced a graphics mod, ReShade, an ENB or another plugin they had installed
- FiveM or its updater replaced or removed a file in the folder (not measured for this folder)
- A clean-up, "clear FiveM cache" or optimiser tool that empties FiveM's folders
- Antivirus software quarantining or removing a file
- FiveM reinstalled, or its folder deleted and made again. Records about the old folder are not counted at all, so this can also remove a row that would otherwise be here

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/change-journal-records>
- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winioctl/ns-winioctl-usn_record_v3>

<a id="rule-7996285e-8ccf-4b2d-8fec-339a32b95931"></a>

- File: [`rules/usn/enhanced-asi/files-renamed/rule.yaml`](../rules/usn/enhanced-asi/files-renamed/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `usn`
- Strength: `context`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `usn`, `enhanced_asi`

The NTFS change journal holds at least one record of a file renamed directly inside FiveM for GTA V Enhanced's asi folder, moved into it or moved out of it. A rename inside the folder leaves two records, one for the old name and one for the new. The row gives how many records, and the first and last time. It shows the span the journal covered: on an ordinary PC in use that can be well under an hour. Nothing before that span is seen. If this rule finds nothing, it means only that nothing was renamed, moved in or moved out there within that span. The journal does not record which program changed a file, so this does not say who did it, or that anything was hidden. Whether FiveM for GTA V Enhanced loads anything from this folder is not established.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `folder`: is `identified` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `location`: is `enhanced_asi` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `renamed|gte`: is at least `1`

**Look-back**

Only the span the change journal still held when the scan read it, shown beside this row. The journal keeps a fixed size and drops its oldest records first; on one Windows 11 PC it held about 39 minutes.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows
- `source_absent` — this PC has no such record to read
- `other_volume` — this is on another drive, and this program reads only the system drive's change journal

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- The player renamed, moved or replaced a graphics mod, ReShade, an ENB or another plugin they had installed
- An update that writes a new copy of a file and swaps it in by renaming, by FiveM, its updater or a plugin (not measured for this folder)
- A file moved to the Recycle Bin or to another folder on the same drive, which the journal records as a rename (how the Recycle Bin shows was not measured)
- Antivirus software quarantining a file
- FiveM reinstalled, or its folder deleted and made again. Records about the old folder are not counted at all, so this can also remove a row that would otherwise be here

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/change-journal-records>
- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winioctl/ns-winioctl-usn_record_v3>

### `usn` / `psreadline`

<a id="rule-926b3863-8f4f-4d18-aab6-26b77934466e"></a>

#### The change journal holds a deletion in PowerShell's command history folder

- Id: `926b3863-8f4f-4d18-aab6-26b77934466e`
- File: [`rules/usn/psreadline/files-deleted/rule.yaml`](../rules/usn/psreadline/files-deleted/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `usn`
- Strength: `context`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `usn`, `psreadline`
- Written: 2026-10-08

**About this check**

The NTFS change journal holds at least one record of a file deleted directly inside the folder where PowerShell keeps the history of commands typed into its window. PowerShell adds to that file and rewrites it, and does not delete it, so a deletion there was made by a person or by another program. The row gives how many records, and the first and last time, never a file name or anything the file held. It shows the span the journal covered: on an ordinary PC in use that can be well under an hour. Nothing before that span is seen, and a deleted folder, rather than a file in it, is not counted. If this rule finds nothing, it means only that nothing was deleted there within that span. The journal does not record which program deleted a file, so this does not say who did it, or that anything was hidden.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `deleted|gte`: is at least `1`
- `folder`: is `identified` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `location`: is `psreadline` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Only the span the change journal still held when the scan read it, shown beside this row. The journal keeps a fixed size and drops its oldest records first; on one Windows 11 PC it held about 39 minutes.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows
- `source_absent` — this PC has no such record to read
- `other_volume` — this is on another drive, and this program reads only the system drive's change journal

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- The player clearing their own PowerShell history, which deletes the file
- A privacy, clean-up or optimiser tool that clears command histories
- A Windows profile reset, or a backup or sync tool restoring the folder
- Antivirus software removing a file from the folder

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/psreadline/about/about_psreadline>
- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/change-journal-records>

- `other_volume` — this is on another drive, and this program reads only the system drive's change journal

## Collector `wmi_subscription`

### `wmi_subscription` / `consumer`

<a id="rule-7a7cebaa-f0ae-4e82-9234-4b53f853eacb"></a>

#### A permanent WMI subscription runs a command line or a script

- Id: `7a7cebaa-f0ae-4e82-9234-4b53f853eacb`
- File: [`rules/wmi_subscription/consumer/command-or-script-consumer/rule.yaml`](../rules/wmi_subscription/consumer/command-or-script-consumer/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `wmi_subscription`
- Strength: `presence`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `persistence`, `wmi`
- Written: 2026-10-15

**About this check**

WMI holds a CommandLineEventConsumer or ActiveScriptEventConsumer that is not one Windows ships: when its event filter fires, Windows starts the program or runs the script by itself, without a logged-in user. The row names the program, the script file or the files the script mentions, and their hash and signature when they exist; the script's text and the command's arguments are never kept. It is a way to start something persistently, not proof of what it starts.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `consumer_kind`: is one of `command_line`, `active_script` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `known_default`: is `false`
- `scope`: is `consumer` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

A subscription lasts until it is deleted; WMI's repository survives restarts.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `access_denied` — Windows refused to open this
- `source_absent` — this PC has no such record to read

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- Hardware vendor and management software (Dell, HP, Lenovo utilities, SCCM/Intune agents) that use WMI subscriptions
- Scripts an IT department or the owner set up for maintenance

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wmisdk/receiving-events-at-all-times>

<a id="rule-2a0c35e1-7d5e-425e-a0f7-99424e7973ec"></a>

#### A permanent WMI subscription names a Roblox executor or injector

- Id: `2a0c35e1-7d5e-425e-a0f7-99424e7973ec`
- File: [`rules/wmi_subscription/consumer/roblox-tool-in-consumer/rule.yaml`](../rules/wmi_subscription/consumer/roblox-tool-in-consumer/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `wmi_subscription`
- Strength: `presence`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `roblox`, `persistence`, `wmi`
- Written: 2026-10-15

**About this check**

A WMI event consumer's name, program, script file or the files its script mentions match a Roblox executor or injector. Windows would start that by itself whenever the subscription's event happens. A name is not proof of what the program is.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `scope`: is `consumer` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `tool_kind`: is one of `executor`, `injector` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

A subscription lasts until it is deleted.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `access_denied` — Windows refused to open this
- `source_absent` — this PC has no such record to read

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- An unrelated program with the same name started by a vendor's WMI subscription

## Timeline selectors

A timeline selector is written like a rule and produces no evidence: the observations it matches put their times on the report's timeline, each with the text and the ordinary causes below. It is never Found, Not found or Not measured, and never counted (ADR 0051). A timeline selector may choose Prefetch, BAM and Program Compatibility Assistant records by name, which a rule may not (ADR 0034): a name says nothing about which program it was, and each one says so.

### `amcache` / `timeline`

<a id="rule-d5560346-9ad6-4b02-ad7b-692097d5bf8a"></a>

#### Times Amcache wrote entries for Roblox tools

- Id: `d5560346-9ad6-4b02-ad7b-692097d5bf8a`
- File: [`rules/amcache/timeline/tool-entry-times/rule.yaml`](../rules/amcache/timeline/tool-entry-times/rule.yaml)
- Role: `timeline` — a timeline selector: its matches are times on the timeline, never evidence
- Collector: `amcache`
- Strength: `context`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `timeline`, `roblox`
- Written: 2026-10-15

**About this check**

Puts on the timeline when Windows' program inventory wrote its entry for a program whose name matches the Roblox tool catalog.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `scope`: is `file` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `tool_id|exists`: the field is present

**Look-back**

Amcache keeps entries for months.

**Ordinary things behind these times**

- An entry's time is when it was written, not a run time

### `bam` / `timeline`

<a id="rule-bf213176-ed26-4c02-935e-99925abc7db7"></a>

#### When BAM recorded a program named like FiveM's game process

- Id: `bf213176-ed26-4c02-935e-99925abc7db7`
- File: [`rules/bam/timeline/fivem-game-process-by-name/rule.yaml`](../rules/bam/timeline/fivem-game-process-by-name/rule.yaml)
- Role: `timeline` — a timeline selector: its matches are times on the timeline, never evidence
- Collector: `bam`
- Strength: `context`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `bam`, `timeline`
- Written: 2026-09-17

**About this check**

Puts on the timeline the time the Windows Background Activity Moderator (BAM) recorded for a program named FiveM\_b\<number\>\_GTAProcess.exe, the name FiveM gives the game process it starts, with the game build in place of \<number\>. The record holds a name, not which program it was, so this shows when a program of that name ran according to this record, not that FiveM or GTA V ran. It is not evidence of anything, and a missing entry does not mean the game never ran.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `name|endswith`: ends with `_GTAProcess.exe` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `name|startswith`: starts with `FiveM_b` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Only what BAM still holds. Windows removes BAM entries older than seven days when it starts, so an older run leaves no entry here.

**Ordinary things behind these times**

- Any program whose name begins with FiveM\_b and ends with \_GTAProcess.exe — the record holds a name and nothing that identifies the program, so a program renamed to that shape is recorded under it
- A program of another name is not selected, whatever it is, so an absent entry does not mean that nothing ran
- Windows not keeping a record — BAM entries older than seven days are removed when Windows starts
- Windows keeping the record after the program's files were removed

Only what BAM still holds. Windows removes BAM entries older than seven days when it starts, so an older run leaves no entry here.

**Ordinary things behind these times**

- Any program of one of these names — the record holds a name and nothing that identifies the program, so a program renamed to one of them is recorded under it
- A program of another name is not selected, whatever it is, so an absent entry does not mean that nothing ran
- Windows not keeping a record — BAM entries older than seven days are removed when Windows starts
- Windows keeping the record after the program's files were removed

### `evtx` / `timeline`

<a id="rule-51bb1937-7ab2-48db-a2f2-78be82ba2fe8"></a>

#### When Code Integrity recorded that Windows refused to load a file

- Id: `51bb1937-7ab2-48db-a2f2-78be82ba2fe8`
- File: [`rules/evtx/timeline/code-integrity-blocked-image/rule.yaml`](../rules/evtx/timeline/code-integrity-blocked-image/rule.yaml)
- Role: `timeline` — a timeline selector: its matches are times on the timeline, never evidence
- Collector: `evtx`
- Strength: `context`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `evtx`, `timeline`
- Written: 2026-09-30

**About this check**

Puts on the timeline the first and last time the Code Integrity log still holds a record of Windows refusing to load a program, a DLL or a driver whose signature did not meet what was required of it. This tool does not read what is inside those records, so a time here does not say which file was refused, which program asked for it or which policy refused it. Windows 11 refuses some files by default, and an ordinary PC measured for this held hundreds of these records. It is not evidence that anything was injected, blocked on purpose or removed.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `channel`: is `Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `event_id`: is one of `3033`, `3077`
- `provider`: is `Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Only the records the Code Integrity log still holds. It keeps about 1 MB by default and overwrites its oldest records when it is full — on an ordinary PC measured for this, about three weeks — and a cleared log holds none.

**Ordinary things behind these times**

- Microsoft's vulnerable driver blocklist, on by default on Windows 11, refusing an old driver that hardware utilities, RGB and fan control, overclocking tools and older anti-cheat software install
- Memory integrity, Smart App Control or S mode refusing a driver or program that does not meet their requirements
- A program that asks Windows to load only Microsoft-signed code into itself (Code Integrity Guard) refusing a DLL that another program tries to place in it — overlays, screen recorders, input tools, antivirus and accessibility software. Which programs on a PC do this is not measured
- A signature that was revoked or has expired on a file the PC still has
- An App Control policy an employer, a school or a PC maker installed
- No time here does not mean nothing was refused before the log's oldest record

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/application-security/application-control/app-control-for-business/operations/event-id-explanations>
- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/application-security/application-control/app-control-for-business/design/microsoft-recommended-driver-block-rules>

<a id="rule-63269014-f728-424c-8e18-e36fe79030aa"></a>

#### When Microsoft Defender recorded a detection

- Id: `63269014-f728-424c-8e18-e36fe79030aa`
- File: [`rules/evtx/timeline/defender-detection/rule.yaml`](../rules/evtx/timeline/defender-detection/rule.yaml)
- Role: `timeline` — a timeline selector: its matches are times on the timeline, never evidence
- Collector: `evtx`
- Strength: `context`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `evtx`, `timeline`
- Written: 2026-09-30

**About this check**

Puts on the timeline the first and last time Microsoft Defender's log still holds a record that it detected malware or potentially unwanted software, or acted on something it detected. This tool does not read what is inside those records, so a time here does not say what was detected, where, or whether it was ever run, and Defender records its own mistakes in the same words. It is not evidence about the file or about the person.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `channel`: is `Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `event_id`: is one of `1116`, `1117`
- `provider`: is `Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Only the records Defender's log still holds. It keeps up to 16 MiB by default and overwrites its oldest records when it is full, and a cleared log holds none.

**Ordinary things behind these times**

- Potentially unwanted software bundled with free programs
- Game trainers, mod tools, key generators and cracked software, which antivirus products flag as unwanted software or hacking tools
- A false positive on a new or unsigned program
- A file that was downloaded and never run
- A detection in a file Defender removed at once
- No time here does not mean Defender detected nothing before the log's oldest record, or that another antivirus did not

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/troubleshoot-microsoft-defender-antivirus>

<a id="rule-87b47713-1ed3-415e-bc07-9cd0b953d7c1"></a>

#### A Windows event log's oldest and newest record

- Id: `87b47713-1ed3-415e-bc07-9cd0b953d7c1`
- File: [`rules/evtx/timeline/log-oldest-and-newest-record/rule.yaml`](../rules/evtx/timeline/log-oldest-and-newest-record/rule.yaml)
- Role: `timeline` — a timeline selector: its matches are times on the timeline, never evidence
- Collector: `evtx`
- Strength: `context`
- Status: `test` — believed correct; has a positive and a negative fixture
- Tags: `evtx`, `timeline`
- Written: 2026-09-17

**About this check**

Puts on the timeline the time of the oldest and the newest record each Windows event log file still holds. The span between them is what that log can show; a time outside it is one the log says nothing about. A short span is not evidence that a log was cleared.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `oldest_record_time|exists`: the field is present

**Look-back**

The log files as they are at the moment of the scan. Each log has a size limit and overwrites its oldest records when it is full.

**Ordinary things behind these times**

- A log that reached its size limit and overwrote its oldest records, which busy logs do within days
- A new Windows installation, or a reset
- A log cleared by an administrator, by an installer or by a maintenance tool

<a id="rule-5bd03528-fcfe-4e57-8a7f-3a2ec815a7af"></a>

#### When PowerShell recorded a script block it considers suspicious

- Id: `5bd03528-fcfe-4e57-8a7f-3a2ec815a7af`
- File: [`rules/evtx/timeline/powershell-flagged-script-block/rule.yaml`](../rules/evtx/timeline/powershell-flagged-script-block/rule.yaml)
- Role: `timeline` — a timeline selector: its matches are times on the timeline, never evidence
- Collector: `evtx`
- Strength: `context`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `evtx`, `timeline`, `powershell`
- Written: 2026-10-08

**About this check**

Puts on the timeline the first and last time Windows PowerShell's operational log still holds a script block that PowerShell itself flagged as suspicious. PowerShell does this even when script block logging is not switched on, for any script containing one of a fixed list of words — among them the ones a script uses to call into Windows, read or write another program's memory, or decode text — and ordinary scripts contain them too. This tool does not read the block, so a time here does not say what the script was, who ran it, or whether it did anything. It is not evidence about the person.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `channel`: is `Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `event_id`: is `4104`
- `level`: is `3`
- `provider`: is `Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Only the blocks the log still holds. It keeps 15 MiB by default and overwrites its oldest records when it is full; on one Windows 11 PC that was about a day and a half. A cleared log holds none.

**Ordinary things behind these times**

- Scripts that show a window or a dialog, install software, or manage Windows, which use the same words
- Administration, development and game tools that run PowerShell in the background
- A script that only contains one of the words as text, such as Bypass
- No time here does not mean no script ran. PowerShell records nothing this way when a policy turns script block logging off, and PowerShell 7 records it in another log, which on one PC measured did not exist; scripts run before the log's oldest record are not seen
- A policy that turns script block logging off, which the PowerShell posture rows report: PowerShell then flags nothing, so no time here says nothing

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_logging_windows>
- <https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/blob/master/src/System.Management.Automation/engine/runtime/CompiledScriptBlock.cs>

### `fivem_dir` / `timeline`

<a id="rule-2ef0da16-e65e-4bb6-90c5-0898ffc93ad8"></a>

#### When FiveM's log, crash and cache folders were written

- Id: `2ef0da16-e65e-4bb6-90c5-0898ffc93ad8`
- File: [`rules/fivem_dir/timeline/folder-activity-times/rule.yaml`](../rules/fivem_dir/timeline/folder-activity-times/rule.yaml)

**About this check**

Puts on the timeline the times FiveM's log, crash and cache folders report, for GTA V Legacy and Enhanced: when each folder was created and last changed, the earliest and latest file times in it, and when each Enhanced server cache folder was created and last changed. These are the times the file system reports, which the program that writes a file can set. A server cache folder is shown without its name. None of this is evidence of anything.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `location`: is one of `legacy_logs`, `legacy_crashes`, `legacy_cache`, `legacy_server_cache`, `enhanced_logs`, `enhanced_crashes`, `enhanced_launcher_crashes`, `enhanced_server_cache` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

The folders as they are at the moment of the scan. FiveM writes, rotates and removes its own logs, crash reports and cache, and a player can clear them.

- FiveM writing, rotating and removing its own logs, crash reports and cache in ordinary use
- The player clearing FiveM's cache or logs
- Reinstalling FiveM, moving it to another PC, or restoring it from a backup

### `pca` / `timeline`

<a id="rule-eaf79187-e067-43ed-9afe-bffe65e6b2e5"></a>

#### When Program Compatibility Assistant recorded a program named like FiveM's game process

- Id: `eaf79187-e067-43ed-9afe-bffe65e6b2e5`
- File: [`rules/pca/timeline/fivem-game-process-by-name/rule.yaml`](../rules/pca/timeline/fivem-game-process-by-name/rule.yaml)
- Role: `timeline` — a timeline selector: its matches are times on the timeline, never evidence
- Collector: `pca`
- Strength: `context`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `pca`, `timeline`
- Written: 2026-09-17

**About this check**

Puts on the timeline the time the Windows Program Compatibility Assistant recorded for a program named FiveM\_b\<number\>\_GTAProcess.exe, the name FiveM gives the game process it starts, with the game build in place of \<number\>. The record holds a name, not which program it was, so this shows when a program of that name ran according to this record, not that FiveM or GTA V ran. It is not evidence of anything, and a missing entry does not mean the game never ran.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `name|endswith`: ends with `_GTAProcess.exe` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `name|startswith`: starts with `FiveM_b` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Only what the Program Compatibility Assistant files still hold. Windows keeps these files on Windows 11 22H2 and later.

**Ordinary things behind these times**

- Any program whose name begins with FiveM\_b and ends with \_GTAProcess.exe — the record holds a name and nothing that identifies the program, so a program renamed to that shape is recorded under it
- A program of another name is not selected, whatever it is, so an absent entry does not mean that nothing ran
- Windows not writing a record — these files exist only on Windows 11 22H2 and later
- Windows keeping the record after the program's files were removed

Only what the Program Compatibility Assistant files still hold. Windows keeps these files on Windows 11 22H2 and later.

### `pci_device` / `timeline`

<a id="rule-f360d84c-0ac6-437c-af21-5193d9264e0f"></a>

#### When Windows recorded a PCI device that is not present now

- Id: `f360d84c-0ac6-437c-af21-5193d9264e0f`
- File: [`rules/pci_device/timeline/absent-device-times/rule.yaml`](../rules/pci_device/timeline/absent-device-times/rule.yaml)
- Role: `timeline` — a timeline selector: its matches are times on the timeline, never evidence
- Collector: `pci_device`
- Strength: `context`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `pci_device`, `timeline`
- Written: 2026-10-15

**About this check**

Puts on the timeline the times Windows stores for each PCI device that is not in the PC now: when it was first set up, the last start of Windows at which it was present, and a removal time when Windows recorded one. Present devices are left out: every one of them last arrived at the start of Windows. A time here is not evidence that anything was removed on purpose.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `present`: is `false`

**Look-back**

Devices Windows still remembers, until a device is uninstalled or Windows is installed again.

**Ordinary things behind these times**

- A part replaced or moved, a BIOS update or setting, or an external PCIe device unplugged
- After a full shutdown Windows records no removal time, so a missing one says nothing about when a device left
- A clock that was changed, so that these times are not on the same clock as the others

### `powershell_text` / `timeline`

<a id="rule-bc3c9769-c57e-4c01-9f0d-8a71152102ec"></a>

#### When PowerShell's logs recorded a command that downloaded something and ran it

- Id: `bc3c9769-c57e-4c01-9f0d-8a71152102ec`
- File: [`rules/powershell_text/timeline/download-then-execute-times/rule.yaml`](../rules/powershell_text/timeline/download-then-execute-times/rule.yaml)
- Role: `timeline` — a timeline selector: its matches are times on the timeline, never evidence
- Collector: `powershell_text`
- Strength: `context`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `powershell_text`
- Written: 2026-10-08

**About this check**

Puts on the timeline the first and last time a flagged script block or a Windows PowerShell start held both a word that downloads and a word that runs text as a command. The history has no times and is not on the timeline. This tool reads the command only to sort its words into kinds and keeps no text of it, so the row says what kind of words it held, never which command, what it ran or whether it worked. A word built some other way than PowerShell's ordinary escapes is not recognised, so a missing row says nothing.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `download_then_execute`: is `true`
- `first_seen|exists`: the field is present

**Look-back**

Only the records the two Windows PowerShell logs still hold; each keeps 15 MiB by default and overwrites its oldest records when full.

**Ordinary things behind these times**

- Installers and update scripts that download and run in one line
- A missing time does not mean nothing ran, and no time before a log's oldest record is seen
- A policy that turns script block logging off, which the PowerShell posture rows report: no flagged block is then written, and only Windows PowerShell's starts can put a time here

**References**

- <https://github.com/aeterna/aeterna-rongroi/blob/dev/docs/adr/0064-words-in-powershell-commands-never-the-commands.md>

**About this check**

Puts on the timeline the times this source records for a program whose file name starts with the name of a publicly discussed Roblox executor. A file name is not an identity: anyone can name a file anything, and several of these names are ordinary words.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `name|startswith`: starts with one of `Solara`, `Xeno`, `Celery`, `Fluxus`, `KRNL`, `JJSploit`, `Synapse`, `Seliware`, `Nihon`, `Script-Ware` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Whatever this source still holds.

**Ordinary things behind these times**

- A file renamed or named this way for an unrelated reason; a name does not identify a program, and a missing time is not evidence of anything

#### Change journal times for files named like Roblox tools

- File: [`rules/usn/timeline/tool-name-records/rule.yaml`](../rules/usn/timeline/tool-name-records/rule.yaml)
- Role: `timeline` — a timeline selector: its matches are times on the timeline, never evidence
- Collector: `usn`
- Strength: `context`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `timeline`, `roblox`
- Written: 2026-10-15

**About this check**

Puts on the timeline the first and last change journal record for each file name that matches the Roblox tool catalog.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `location`: is `named` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

The change journal keeps a bounded number of recent records.

**Ordinary things behind these times**

- A name is not a file identity

<a id="rule-82c71896-ef70-492d-b6fc-8671c09b5e1c"></a>

#### When the change journal recorded changes in a watched folder

- Id: `82c71896-ef70-492d-b6fc-8671c09b5e1c`
- File: [`rules/usn/timeline/watched-folder-record-times/rule.yaml`](../rules/usn/timeline/watched-folder-record-times/rule.yaml)
- Role: `timeline` — a timeline selector: its matches are times on the timeline, never evidence
- Collector: `usn`
- Strength: `context`
- Status: `test` — believed correct; has a positive and a negative fixture
- Tags: `usn`, `timeline`
- Written: 2026-09-17

**About this check**

Puts on the timeline the oldest and newest change the NTFS change journal still holds for each folder this program watches: Prefetch, the event log folder, the Program Compatibility Assistant folder, FiveM's plugin folders and the folder PowerShell keeps its command history in. The journal counts changes without saying which program made them, so a time here is when a file in that folder was created, changed, renamed or deleted, by anyone, including Windows and FiveM; in PowerShell's folder a change is usually a command typed into a PowerShell window, never which command. It is not evidence that anything was removed.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `folder`: is `identified` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Only the records the journal still holds. The journal has a fixed size and drops its oldest records as new ones arrive, so it reaches back only as far as its size allows.

**Ordinary things behind these times**

- Windows writing and removing Prefetch files, event logs and compatibility records in ordinary use
- FiveM, its updater and plugins installed or removed by the player changing files in the plugin folders
- PowerShell adding each command typed into its window to its history file
- Disk clean-up, backup, antivirus and optimisation tools
- A folder with no change in the journal's span has no time here, which does not mean nothing changed before it

### `windows_start` / `timeline`

<a id="rule-fe57aa65-11b0-4e1f-b81c-a4fda597855b"></a>

#### Windows started after a Fast Startup shutdown

- Id: `fe57aa65-11b0-4e1f-b81c-a4fda597855b`
- File: [`rules/windows_start/timeline/fast-startup-start/rule.yaml`](../rules/windows_start/timeline/fast-startup-start/rule.yaml)
- Role: `timeline` — a timeline selector: its matches are times on the timeline, never evidence
- Collector: `windows_start`
- Strength: `context`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `windows_start`, `timeline`
- Written: 2026-10-15

**About this check**

Puts on the timeline each start of Windows that its System log records with boot type 1, which was measured after a shutdown with Fast Startup on, the default. A device taken out while Windows was off this way has a removal time, written during the shutdown, and the start of Windows does not write its arrival times again.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `boot_type`: is `1`

**Look-back**

As long as the System log keeps its records: by default it overwrites the oldest when it reaches its size.

**Ordinary things behind these times**

- Fast Startup is on by default, so most shutdowns from the Start menu end this way

<a id="rule-fa3e721e-98f2-4007-bbd8-133208564682"></a>

#### Windows started after a full shutdown or a restart

- Id: `fa3e721e-98f2-4007-bbd8-133208564682`
- File: [`rules/windows_start/timeline/full-start/rule.yaml`](../rules/windows_start/timeline/full-start/rule.yaml)
- Role: `timeline` — a timeline selector: its matches are times on the timeline, never evidence
- Collector: `windows_start`
- Strength: `context`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `windows_start`, `timeline`
- Written: 2026-10-15

**About this check**

Puts on the timeline each start of Windows that its System log records with boot type 0, which was measured after a full shutdown and after a restart. A device taken out while Windows was off this way has no removal time; the last start at which it was present is all Windows keeps of when it left.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `boot_type`: is `0`

**Look-back**

As long as the System log keeps its records: by default it overwrites the oldest when it reaches its size.

**Ordinary things behind these times**

- Every PC starts this way; a start is a reference point for the other times, not a finding
